title: Microtask Orchestrator - scratchlog
content:
Context and elevator:
- Problem: multi-turn, complex user queries (e.g., document edits, data transformation, multi-step planning) often have internal subtasks. We pay full sequential inference cost and high latency because we treat the whole request as one monolithic generation.
- Goal: reduce perceived latency and token cost by decomposing the work into microtasks we can: (a) prefetch embeddings/KV, (b) parallelize compatible subtasks onto different model pools, (c) apply lightweight heuristics to short-circuit or cache results.

High-level idea: Microtask Orchestrator (MTO)
- When a request comes in, run a fast "decomposer" step (cheap model or deterministic rules) that outputs a small DAG of microtasks with metadata: {type, estimated cost, dependencies, session-affinity, priority}.
- Scheduler maps microtasks to lanes: low-latency lane (small fast quantized model), batching lane (throughput-optimized), or background lane (cheap, non-blocking ops).
- Execute independent microtasks in parallel; stream partial results back to the client as they complete. Use prefix/KV caching aggressively for repeated subtasks.

Why this is interesting for Redwood:
- Plays to our strengths: serving runtime with batching, smart routing, prefix/KV caching, and model catalog diversity.
- Can reduce tail latency for complex flows while also lowering token cost through micro-caching.
- Adds a new routing primitive (microtask affinity + dependency scheduling) that we can expose to Dedicated/Private customers for fine-grained SLAs.

Rough user stories:
- As a search assistant product, I want the system to identify which parts of a query can be answered from cached facts so that the user sees a partial answer quickly.
- As a chat user, I want my long planning prompt to show interim bullet points while the full plan is still being composed.
- As a platform engineer, I want to control which microtask types run on dedicated capacity to guarantee latency for the high-priority pieces.

Prototype approach (MVP):
1) Decomposer: lightweight LLM prompt + heuristics that output a 3–8 microtask list. Minimal schema: id, type (generate/lookup/transform), deps, est_tokens, session_hint.
2) Scheduler: single-node prototype that maps to two lanes: FAST (small model e.g., quantized 7B) and FULL (baseline model). Simple rules: lookups -> FAST, single-turn summarization -> FAST if est_tokens < 64, otherwise FULL.
3) Client streaming: stream microtask completions as JSON "micro-reply" envelopes; final aggregation step stitches them into the canonical response.

Acceptance criteria for prototype:
- End-to-end latency reduction on 50th and 95th percentile for our internal "multi-step planning" dataset by >=20% compared to baseline single-run generation.
- No more than 5% drop in final output quality (measured by our eval prompts) vs baseline.
- Can route at least two microtask types to the FAST lane without catastrophic hallucination in lookup-like microtasks.

Experiments to run:
- Ablation: decomposer quality vs overall gains (use deterministic rules baseline, distilled tiny LLM, and medium LLM)
- Routing policies: cost-first vs latency-first vs hybrid; measure cost per request and user-visible latency
- Caching heuristics: prefix vs microtask result cache TTLs (1m, 1h, 24h)
- Failure modes: if FAST lane returns inconsistent/partial answers, how to reconcile with FULL lane (merge strategies: prefer FULL, merge heuristically, ask clarifying microtask)

Edge cases and risks:
- Decomposer introduces errors that change problem semantics -> can reduce quality. Need conservative defaults and sandboxed rollout.
- Increased system complexity: debugging/fault histograms will need new telemetry (microtask trace ids, per-microtask latency/cost, stitch errors).
- Storage/caching cost: micro-caches could grow; require eviction heuristics keyed by session and microtask fingerprint.

Telemetry & metrics required:
- Per-request microtask DAG size distribution
- P95 microtask execution latency (by lane)
- Re-stitch failure rate (stitch couldn’t assemble coherent final response)
- Cost delta per request and tokens saved by cache hits
- Quality regressions by microtask type (micro-evals)

Rollout plan ideas:
- Alpha: internal-only, opt-in header X-Use-MTO, limited to 10% of internal traffic. Manual vetting of top failure cases.
- Beta: customer opt-in for Hosted API with experimental flag; provide visibility in Console to map microtask types to lanes and cost implications.
- GA: expose orchestration config in Dedicated and Private via a lightweight policy file (json) to pin microtask types to model families and set lane priorities.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Decomposer schema: exact fields and stable spec (needs design).
- Safety: which microtask types are safe to run on small models? Build a whitelist with evals.
- API surface: how to expose partial streaming vs single final response? Backwards compatible?
- SDK ergonomics: offer an SDK helper that transforms micro-replies into convenient client-level partials (JS/py).
- Cost model: how to price microtask execution and streaming (per-token still? per-microtask?).

Notes from convo with Marco (2025-10-14):
- Marco: prioritize deterministic lookups first (KB, embeddings) — biggest win for latency.
- Tess: we must ensure traceability for compliance customers — every microtask needs an audit id.
- Isha: evaluation harness should include user-perceived satisfaction (human evals) because partial replies can change perception even if final quality equals baseline.

Relevant links / references:
- Lightweight decomposition paper notes (local): github.com/redwood-research/decomp-notes
- Internal eval deck: CONFLUENCE-RT-7782 (linked above)

Immediate next steps (me, Zavier):
- Draft decomposer schema & quick rule-based decomposer prototype (1 week)
- Wire simple scheduler in the runtime sandbox and run 1000 internal traces to collect DAG size and savings numbers (2 weeks)
- Set up minimal telemetry (microtask-id, lane, latency, tokens) and dashboard stub in Console (Tess can help)

Quick sketch of a decomposer output example (proto):
[
  {id: "m1", type: "lookup", deps: [], est_tokens: 12, hint: "kb:customer-faqs"},
  {id: "m2", type: "summarize", deps: ["m1"], est_tokens: 40, hint: "summarize-kb+user-prompt"},
  {id: "m3", type: "plan-steps", deps: ["m2"], est_tokens: 120, hint: "expand-planning"}
]

Notes-to-self style: keep MVP small. focus on lookups + short summaries first. Don't over-index on multi-model parallelism in MVP — complexity explosion.

-- Zavier
